primary_topics: Keynote speaker and inducting officer at the MAP 2010 Board of Governors induction, January 26, 2010 -- MAP theme: Principled Leadership in Challenging Times
TIP framework: Trust, Integrity and Probity -- three core values rearranged into a memorable three-letter keyword for leadership in challenging times

Three kinds of government officials: (1) those who arrogate power and plunder; (2) those who are personally pure under abusive regimes; (3) those with integrity who also punish the greedy, chase robbers, and prosecute tyrants -- the third type is what the country needs

Trust as democratic essence: the Philippines declined from the envy of Asia (1950s: P2/dollar) to backwater (2010: P50/dollar); OFWs flourish in democracies like the US and Canada; trust is the essence of good governance in a democracy
sub_topics: CJP's MAP connection: active member before joining SC in 1995; elected to Board of Governors 1990-1994; reuniting with 'the most important management group in the country'

Archbishop's homily on the two commandments: Ten Commandments reduced to love God and love neighbor; then unpacked: 'Shall we just feed the hungry but not punish the greedy who deprived them of food? Shall we just provide clothing without chasing the robbers who stole the clothes? Shall we just visit the prisoners without bringing to justice the tyrants who jailed them?'

Three kinds of officials: (1) arrogate power, plunder, use public office for ill-gotten wealth; (2) serve under abusive regimes but keep personally pure; (3) men and women of integrity who not only refuse to tell falsehoods but have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants'

Trust: in the 1950s-60s, Philippines was the envy of Asia (P2 = $1); 50 years later, almost P50 = $1 (sunk more than 20 times); some propose following Singapore, South Korea, Vietnam's authoritarian models -- CJP disagrees: 'the Philippines is not Singapore; during the martial law years, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress'

OFW-as-democracy-proof: 'Look at the Filipinos abroad. They strictly follow the law. They stop at red lights even in deserted street corners. They honor their obligations. They pay their taxes willingly. They are industrious and productive. In democratic societies like the United States and Canada, our people flourish.'
Trust as democratic essence: 'in a democracy, the essence of good governance is the trust of the people. Once trust is lost, conflict, stagnation and degeneration ensue.'

Probity: Webster defines it as 'uncompromising adherence to the highest principles or ideals'; CJP adds: 'the ability to discern various alternatives and to select the best in a given set of circumstances'; the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons
TIP acronym: trust, integrity and probity rearranged to form TIP; 'my TIP on how to meet the challenges of these times, my TIP on how to win the future'

Jesus as the leadership model: Last Supper, washing of feet; 'If I, the master and teacher, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another's feet. I have given you a model to follow.'; TIP values must be led by example

stances.claim: The country needs the third kind of government official -- not just someone who is personally honest (second kind) but someone with integrity: moral courage to 'punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants.' The distinction between honesty (passive virtue) and integrity (active virtue requiring moral courage) is CJP's most important public service governance contribution in this address.
stances.rhetorical_move: honesty-vs-integrity distinction: passive personal purity vs. active moral courage to confront wrongdoing; the third type of official as the necessary condition for governance recovery
stances.confidence: asserted as the governing governance prescription

stances.claim: OFWs who stop at red lights 'even in deserted street corners' in the US and Canada -- but not at home -- prove that the problem of governance is not with the Filipino character but with the domestic environment of trust and rule enforcement. Filipinos flourish in democracies. The solution is not Singapore-style authoritarianism but rebuilding democratic trust.
stances.rhetorical_move: OFW-as-democracy-proof: Filipino behavior abroad as the empirical refutation of the claim that Filipinos need authoritarianism to be disciplined

notable_anecdotes: The archbishop's unpacking of love: the homily expanded 'love thy neighbor' to expose its justice dimension -- 'Shall we just feed the hungry but not punish the greedy who deprived them of food? Shall we just provide clothing without chasing the robbers who stole the clothes?' -- making love actively just rather than passively charitable.

The P2-to-P50 decline: Philippines went from the envy of Asia (P2/$1 in the 1950s) to the backwater (almost P50/$1 fifty years later) -- 'the exchange rate has sunk more than 20 times.' This is CJP's most direct statement of national economic failure.

Red lights in deserted corners: 'Look at the Filipinos abroad. They strictly follow the law. They stop at red lights even in deserted street corners.' -- the most succinct proof that the Filipino character is not the problem; the domestic institutional environment is.

Jesus washing feet as leadership model: 'If I, the master and teacher, have washed your feet, you too ought to wash one another's feet. I have given you a model to follow.' -- the ultimate servant-leadership illustration applied to the MAP's management audience.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered January 26, 2010 as keynote speaker and inducting officer at the MAP 2010 Board of Governors induction -- on the MAP theme 'Principled Leadership in Challenging Times' -- this address by CJP (a former MAP Board member from 1990-1994) presents the TIP framework: Trust, Integrity and Probity. He opens with an archbishop's homily unpacking 'love thy neighbor' into its justice dimension: 'Shall we just feed the hungry but not punish the greedy who deprived them of food? Shall we just provide clothing without chasing the robbers who stole the clothes?' He distinguishes three kinds of government officials: (1) those who arrogate power and plunder; (2) those who are personally pure under abusive regimes -- honesty being 'a virtue taught in grade school'; (3) those with integrity who have 'the moral courage to punish the greedy, chase the robbers, and prosecute the tyrants' -- what the country needs in challenging times. On trust: the Philippines went from the envy of Asia in the 1950s (P2 = $1) to the backwater of Asia (almost P50 = $1, 'the exchange rate has sunk more than 20 times in 50 years'). Those who propose Singapore-style authoritarianism are wrong -- 'the Philippines is not Singapore; during the martial law years, authoritarian rule was proven to be incapable of producing meaningful long-term economic progress.' The proof: 'Look at the Filipinos abroad. They strictly follow the law. They stop at red lights even in deserted street corners. They honor their obligations. They pay their taxes willingly.' In democratic societies like the US and Canada, Filipinos flourish -- because 'in a democracy, the essence of good governance is the trust of the people.' On probity: Webster's 'uncompromising adherence to the highest principles or ideals,' plus CJP's addition -- 'the ability to discern alternatives and select the best' -- in short, 'do the right thing in the right way at the right time and for the right reasons.' He recombines the three values into the TIP mnemonic ('my TIP on how to meet the challenges of these times') and closes with Jesus washing his disciples' feet at the Last Supper: 'I have given you a model to follow... leading by example is the best, if not the only, way to long-term and effective leadership.'
